entities.name: Old City of Jerusalem
entities.label: Place
entities.summary:
The Old City of Jerusalem, a 0.9-square-kilometre (0.35 sq mi) walled area within modern East Jerusalem, stands as a crucible of Abrahamic faiths and a contested geopolitical prize for over three millennia. Its profound significance derives from being home to sites revered by Jews (Western Wall, Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif), Christians (Church of the Holy Sepulchre), and Muslims (Dome of the Rock, Al-Aqsa Mosque), making it a focal point for pilgrimage, devotion, and conflict across successive empires. From its earliest fortifications during the Middle Bronze Age (c. 1800 BCE) to its pivotal role in Roman, Byzantine, Crusader, Ottoman, and modern Israeli-Palestinian narratives, the Old City has continuously shaped religious identity, political ambition, and cultural heritage on a global scale.

The physical fabric of the Old City reflects layers of conquest and reconstruction. King David is traditionally credited with establishing Jerusalem as the capital of the United Monarchy around 1000 BCE, while King Solomon built the First Temple on the Temple Mount. Following its destruction by Nebuchadnezzar II in 586 BCE, the Second Temple was erected and later magnificently expanded by Herod the Great in the 1st century BCE. The Roman destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE, after the Great Jewish Revolt, marked a profound turning point, leading to the city's renaming as Aelia Capitolina and the construction of new Roman urban plans. Subsequent Byzantine rule saw the flourishing of Christian pilgrimage and monumental church building, notably under Emperor Constantine I, only to be challenged by the Persian Sasanian conquest in 614 CE and the decisive Muslim conquest under Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab in 637 CE, which ushered in centuries of Islamic governance, marked by the construction of the Dome of the Rock and Al-Aqsa Mosque.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Old City of Jerusalem holds unparalleled historical significance as a central sacred site for billions across Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, directly shaping millennia of religious identity, geopolitical conflict, and cultural exchange. Its continuous habitation and contestation have profoundly influenced the trajectory of Middle Eastern and global history.
